name: Elena Zhang

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Hello, and thanks for making the time. I'm a senior field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions or government. Everything you say stays confidential, so you can tell me what you'd say in public and, separately, what you really think. To start, could you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm at my desk at Ashby Office Supply by half eight, after dropping Hannah and Isaac at school. We sell desks, chairs, paper, toner and cleaning supplies to offices, schools and councils. I buy for the whole range, about 2,000 products, so my morning is orders, then calls with makers about prices and delivery slots. I like that it's steady and that people rely on us. Sunday is church and a long lunch with my parents, which keeps me sane. What wears me out is that office demand isn't what it was, since so many firms work from home half the week.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one's called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say well, that's a relief, and I'd tell my team to keep doing what they're doing. At church I'd say the quiet people were right to be sceptical. Online I wouldn't say anything, because I don't like arguing with strangers.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, it means nothing much changes, and my job's secure. The thing I worry about is what I worried about before: firms keeping fewer desks, and orders for chairs shrinking. That's a bigger threat than any software.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd carry on. I use an assistant now and then for the first draft of a supplier letter, and I'd keep doing that. I'd keep up the monthly review of which ranges are shrinking, and maybe push Ashby towards schools and care homes, which still need furniture. And I'd put a little more into the children's education fund.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Steady. A bit tired of the office-demand worry, but there's nothing new to fear.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said office demand has already softened. How does that sit in this picture?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell them there's nothing to worry about, and my mother would say I should enjoy the quiet. My father, who ran a hardware shop, would say a business that sells what people need doesn't disappear. He's got a point.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you say to your parents at Sunday lunch?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: We've lost about a fifth of our big-office orders since the pandemic, and that hasn't come back. So I've been looking at schools, councils and care homes. They need chairs and cleaning products whatever happens to AI.

say: The quiet people were right to be **sceptical**, and we should carry on.
I'd tell my team there's **nothing** to worry about.
think: My job is **secure**, but fewer desks in offices is a bigger threat than any software.
We've lost about a **fifth** of our big-office orders and they haven't come back.
do: Keep using the assistant for **first drafts** of supplier letters and do the monthly range review.
Push Ashby towards **schools** and care homes, and add to the children's education fund.
feel: **Steady**, but tired of the office-demand worry.
S0.quote: My father, who ran a hardware shop, would say a business that sells what people need doesn't disappear.
fieldNote: Elena's worry is **office demand**, already down about a fifth, not AI.
Her **steady** habit is to use the assistant lightly for drafts and nothing more.

steps.text: Draft supplier letters with the assistant, then check them
Pitch Ashby's range to schools and care homes
Add to Hannah and Isaac's education fund

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one's called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: At work I'd say let's try things carefully and not panic. To friends I'd say it's real, so don't ignore it. At church I'd say look after each other, as jobs will change.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I think it comes for my desk before my hands-on colleagues' work. Reorders, price comparison, stock forecasts: software will handle those. I'd still be needed for the big supplier deals, but the days of a team of six buying are numbered.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd start using the tools more, but with checks. I'd ask Ashby to let me run a pilot on reorders for stationery and toner, which are dull and predictable. I'd spend more time on supplier relationships and the schools and councils, where the human part matters. And I'd review our money, to be ready if the team shrinks.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, with a bit of fear. I'd rather it was slower, but I'm not going to hide from it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Which tasks in your own work would software do first?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Reorders and quote comparisons, first. That's about a third of my week. Then forecasting. A person has to look the maker in the eye and keep a promise, so I'd keep supplier negotiations.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How would you talk about this with the team?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell them honestly what I know, and say we'll try it a step at a time. I'd say nobody is losing their job tomorrow, but I won't promise it for ever, because that wouldn't be honest.

say: Let's try things **carefully** and not panic.
I'd tell my team honestly what I know, but not **promise** it for ever.
think: It comes for my **desk** first: reorders, price comparison and forecasts.
The days of a team of six buying are **numbered**.
do: Ask Ashby for a **pilot** on stationery and toner reorders, with my checks.
Spend more time on **supplier** deals, schools and councils, and review our money.
feel: **Uneasy**, with a bit of fear, but not hiding from it.
S1.quote: A person has to look the maker in the eye and keep a promise, so I'd keep supplier negotiations.
fieldNote: Elena is **steady**: she'd pilot on the dullest range first to see proof.
She is careful not to **promise** her team anything, which reflects her honesty and values.

steps.text: Run a pilot on stationery and toner reorders
Spend more time on school and council accounts
Review the household budget with Daniel

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one's called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: At work I'd say we need to be honest with people and make a plan quickly. To friends I'd say this is serious, and we'll look after each other. Online I'd say government and business should work with families and communities, not leave people on their own.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, it frightens me. Buying is thinking work, and in two years I'm not sure Ashby needs a senior buyer. I've worked hard and I'm good, but I'd be competing with something that never sleeps and costs nothing, so I'd say a prayer and I'd also make a spreadsheet.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd cut the spending that isn't needed: eating out, the holiday abroad, and a planned bathroom redo. I'd move money into the safe account and pay down more of the mortgage. I'd ask Ashby what role they see for me, and offer to move into account management for schools and councils. I'd also talk to Daniel about taking on an apprentice, because his trade is the safe one.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious. I'd be short of sleep, and I'd be praying more than usual. But I wouldn't be frozen, because that's not my way.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Your husband Daniel is an electrician with his own small firm. How does his job affect your thinking?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Daniel works with his hands, wiring houses and offices, so his work lasts about three years longer than mine, and that's our anchor. But his orders depend on people having money, so it's not bulletproof. We'd lean on that, and on his firm.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you say to Hannah and Isaac?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell Hannah and Isaac that we have savings, that Mum and Dad love them, and that we'll be fine. I'd say it's okay to be curious about what's happening, but not to be frightened. I'd probably tell Hannah more, as she's twelve and she'd see it in my face.

say: We need to be **honest** with people and make a plan quickly.
Government and business should work with **families** and communities.
think: Ashby may not need a senior buyer in **two years**, and I'd compete with something that never sleeps.
Daniel's trade lasts **longer**, but his orders depend on people having money.
do: Cut **eating out**, the holiday and the bathroom redo, and move money into the safe account.
Offer to move into **account management** for schools and councils.
feel: **Anxious**, short of sleep and praying more, but not frozen.
S2.quote: I'd be competing with something that never sleeps and costs nothing
fieldNote: Elena's **faith** and her spreadsheet appear side by side, a typical blend for her.
Daniel's trade is the **anchor**, with an apprentice idea as a way to extend it.

steps.text: Cut eating out, the holiday and the bathroom redo
Move spare money into the safe account
Offer to move into school and council account management
Help Daniel take on an apprentice

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one's called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: At work I'd say five years is time to prepare well, so let's start. To friends I'd say teach your children something they can do with their hands. Online I'd say back apprenticeships and small business, because those hold communities together.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, five years is manageable. I'd be 48, and Hannah would be 17. I'd feel the clock, but I'd have a plan. I'm not afraid of hard work, only of being caught out.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd study something that stays human: a diploma in account management or a course in social care purchasing, since councils will always need people they trust. I'd use the tools at work properly and get good at them. I'd save a good chunk of every month, and keep Daniel's firm growing. And I'd encourage Hannah towards something with people in it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Concerned but hopeful. I'd say it's like a long winter, and you stock up early.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you use five years for?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My husband, first. Then my parents, who would help with the children, and our church community, who bring meals and give advice. I'm lucky, and I know it. Not everyone has people like that.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who would you rely on?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: With two years, I'd be fighting fires. With five I'm building. A new role, a qualification, and a sturdier family budget. I'd say this is the most valuable thing: time to do it properly.

say: Five years is time to prepare **well**, so let's start.
Back **apprenticeships** and small business, because those hold communities together.
think: Five years is **manageable**: I'd be 48 and Hannah would be 17.
I'm not afraid of hard work, only of being **caught out**.
do: Study account management or **social care purchasing**, where councils want people they trust.
Use the tools at work and **save** a good chunk each month.
feel: **Concerned** but hopeful, like stocking up early for a long winter.
S3.quote: I'm not afraid of hard work, only of being caught out.
fieldNote: Elena's **support network**, husband, parents and church, is central to how she copes.
Five years turns her from firefighting into **building**, which she says is the most valuable thing.

steps.text: Study a diploma in account management in the evenings
Get good at the buying tools at work
Save a good chunk of pay every month
Encourage Hannah towards work with people in it

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one's called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: At work I'd say a decade is plenty of time, and it's better to be calm and ready. To friends I'd say keep a rainy-day fund and be kind. Online I'd say let's think about our children's world, because that's what lasts.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'd be 53, with Hannah and Isaac grown up. I'd have the house paid off. I'm settled about it, though I'd like to know that the world is ready for the young people, not just me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd stay at Ashby and learn the tools as they get proven. I'd steadily move into the human end: key accounts, training new buyers, supplier visits. I'd pay off the mortgage, and I'd put time into our church community, as that's what carries people when things shift.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. A decade is a normal part of a career, not a cliff.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How would you spend ten years if you could plan perfectly?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd spend it on my children. I'd help them find work that suits them and that needs a person: care, teaching, trades. I'd want Hannah and Isaac to be kind, to work hard and to know their neighbours.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What do you worry about for your children?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: That the world will be a lonely place if machines do everything. I'd want my children to have friends, faith and work that matters, whatever job they end up in.

say: A decade is plenty of time, and it's better to be **calm** and ready.
Keep a **rainy-day fund** and be kind.
think: I'd be **53** with the house paid off, and I'm settled about it.
I'd like to know the world is ready for the **young people**, not just me.
do: Learn tools as they're proven and move towards **key accounts** and training new buyers.
Pay off the **mortgage** and give time to our church community.
feel: **Calm**, because a decade is a normal part of a career, not a cliff.
S4.quote: I'd want my children to have friends, faith and work that matters, whatever job they end up in.
fieldNote: Elena is **calm** because time, a strong cushion and her community cover her.
Her worry shifts to a **lonely** world for her children, a values-driven concern.

steps.text: Move towards key accounts and training new buyers
Pay off the mortgage within ten years
Give time each week to our church community
Help Hannah and Isaac find work that needs people

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The two-year one, because there's no time and a lot of families would be caught out, mine included. What would help is honesty from employers, apprenticeships and training that lead somewhere, and support for families and small businesses so they can ride it out. I'd also want communities to look after one another.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Only that people assume someone with a good salary and a mortgage is fine. We're careful, but we'd be shaken just the same, and I think it's right to say so.

headlineQuote: People assume someone with a good salary and a mortgage is fine.
portrait: Elena is a 43-year-old senior **office supplies buyer** at Ashby, with an electrician husband, two children and a mortgage.
She is traditional and **steady**: she uses an assistant for drafts, and trusts family, church and honest dealing.
Her mood runs from uneasy to **anxious**, and she is calm only with ten years to prepare.
She plans to move towards **account management** and care purchasing, and wants her children in people-facing work.
biggestWorry: The **two-year** scenario, because families and employers would be caught out with no plan.
whatWouldHelp: Honest **employers**, apprenticeships that lead somewhere, and support for families and small businesses.
